overview.headline: Radioactive waste types, hazards, storage and disposal methods

keyPoints.point: Waste has two broad classifications called high-level and low-level waste.
keyPoints.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyPoints.point: The fission products account for most heat and penetrating radiation in waste.
keyPoints.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyPoints.point: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives where radioactivity will decay over years.
keyPoints.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyPoints.point: Pool water will shield radiation and cool rods while deep enough for protection.
keyPoints.quote: The water is typically about 40 feet deep and serves both to shield the radiation and cool the rods.

keyTerms.gloss: spent fuel removed from reactors after use
keyTerms.quote: High-level waste is primarily spent fuel removed from reactors after producing electricity.

keyTerms.gloss: contaminated materials from reactor operations and medical uses
keyTerms.quote: Low-level waste comes from reactor operations and from medical, academic, industrial, and other commercial uses of radioactive materials.

keyTerms.gloss: lighter isotopes that create heat and penetrating radiation
keyTerms.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: heavier-than-uranium elements that take longer to decay
keyTerms.quote: These heavier-than-uranium, or "transuranic," elements do not produce nearly the amount of heat

keyTerms.gloss: period measured in years for material to decay
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,000 years.

keyTerms.gloss: deep water pools that store spent fuel for shielding and cooling
keyTerms.quote: All U.S. nuclear power plants store spent nuclear fuel in "spent fuel pools."
